 Android earthquake alerts arrive in Italy, how Google's phone-based warning works
 Google has switched on Android Earthquake Alerts in Italy from November 19: magnitude 4.5 threshold, three alert levels and no app to install. How it works and where it falls short.

 As of November 19, 2026, Android phones in Italy can warn their owners when a quake with an estimated magnitude of 4.5 or higher is under way nearby. Google has switched on the Android Earthquake Alerts System in the country, with no app to install and no sign-up. Italy joins the more than 200 regions worldwide already covered.
 Italy was the missing piece. On October 15 the Mountain View giant took the service from 98 to more than 200 countries and territories, listing Panama and Guatemala among the newcomers , yet in the settings of Italian phones the alerts screen kept showing a "not supported in this region" label. The post published on November 19 on the Italian edition of Google's blog , signed by Boone Spooner (Group Product Manager on the Earthquake Alerts team), settles the matter.
 The system debuted in 2021 in New Zealand and Greece and, according to Google, has sent more than a billion alerts since. To receive them you need an Android phone with Google services, a connection (Wi-Fi or mobile data) and location turned on.
 The three alert levels of Android's earthquake warning system, now live in Italy too. 
 Try it now 
 On your Android phone open Settings, then Safety & emergency, then Earthquake alerts. The "See a demo" option shows what the three alerts look like. You need a phone with Google services, and the feature is free and already switched on by default.
 Official Google guide 
 What changes today on Italian phones
 The rollout runs server-side through Google Play Services, the system app that updates itself, so most users have nothing to download. The "Earthquake Alerts isn't available" badge disappears and the page with the three alert levels shows up, as TuttoAndroid checked.
 November 19 is the date Google gave for reaching nearly all compatible devices. It is a rollout date, not a guarantee that every phone is ready, as Tom's Hardware points out. The outlet had found Google's Italian-language guide still missing Italy from the list of supported territories earlier in the morning (the English one already included it). Later in the day the support page appears to be aligned.
 Google keeps bringing services to Italy one after another, following the digital passport in Google Wallet in October. The alerts stay on by default and can be turned off from the same page. To stop contributing to detection as well, in other words to stop acting as a sensor, Google's guide says to switch off Google Location Accuracy.
 How Android's Earthquake Alerts Work
 Android's alerts rely on phone accelerometers. A stationary phone that feels the P wave, the fastest one, sends Google a signal with its approximate location. If many nearby devices agree, the server estimates epicenter and magnitude and warns anyone about to be hit by the S wave, slower and more destructive.
 The system does not predict earthquakes. It detects them once the shaking has begun, and how much notice is left depends on distance. In the magnitude 6.7 Philippines quake of November 2023 the first alert went out 18.3 seconds after the shaking started, people closest to the epicenter got up to 15 seconds, and those who felt only moderate shaking got as much as a minute, according to the Google Research blog . In Nepal, for a magnitude 5.7 quake also in November 2023, more than 10 million alerts were delivered.
 The groundwork is a study published in Science in July 2025, which engineer Marc Stogaitis summarized on the Google Research blog. Google says it has detected more than 18,000 earthquakes, from magnitude 1.9 to 7.8. For more than 2,000 of those events it sent alerts, 790 million in all. Over the same period the median error of the first magnitude estimate reportedly fell from 0.50 to 0.25, a figure the company compares to that of traditional seismic networks.
 The Three Alert Levels and the Magnitude 4.5 Threshold
 Notifications cover quakes with an estimated magnitude of 4.5 or higher. Below that threshold the phone says nothing, even if you feel the shaking. Above it, the system picks one of three levels based on the shaking intensity expected where the user is.
 Level When it triggers What the phone does 
 Be Aware Estimated light shaking nearby Vibration and notification, no sound 
 Be Ready Stronger shaking you should prepare for Sound, vibration and detailed notification 
 Take Action Moderate to strong shaking Full screen, loud sound, instructions for getting to safety 
 The most serious alert is also the most intrusive. As Tom's Hardware notes, Take Action can override Do Not Disturb, wake the screen and ring at full volume, while Be Aware stays a discreet notification that may go unnoticed. In the coming months Be Ready changes too, with a map of the radius where shaking was detected, the estimated magnitude, recommended actions and a button to receive updates as they come in.
 A magnitude 5.5 quake, like the one that on October 23 triggered the tsunami alert in Sicily after the earthquake in the Aeolian Islands , sits one point above the threshold. An event that size falls squarely within the service's scope.
 Limitations to keep in mind 
 The effectiveness figures were measured by Google itself, namely the billion alerts, the 790 million in the study and the 85% of "very helpful" ratings out of 1.5 million responses to the survey embedded in the alerts. For Italy there is still no independent data because the service is only starting, so accuracy on Italian quakes remains to be seen.
 The system has already missed badly. For the magnitude 7.8 quake in Turkey on February 6, 2023 the first estimate was 4.5-4.9 and only 469 people received the most urgent alert, against the roughly 10 million reachable according to the simulation Google admitted to . The error has dropped since, but in the first seconds of a big quake the estimate can still come in lower than the real thing.
 Advance notice is not guaranteed, since the alert can arrive before, during or after the shaking starts, and estimates can contain errors. With the phone on silent a Be Aware alert can go unnoticed.
 IT-alert and Android, Two Different Tools
 Italy already has a public warning system, IT-alert, run by the Department of Civil Protection. It sends a message to every phone in an area through mobile network cells, no app required. The list of cases it covers, in the February 2023 directive described on the system's website , includes a tsunami generated by an earthquake, the collapse of a large dam, activity at the volcanoes Vesuvius, Campi Flegrei, Vulcano and Stromboli, nuclear or radiological accidents, major industrial accidents and heavy rain. The earthquake itself is not on the list.
 The two do not replace each other. IT-alert is the state's official channel, with an authority deciding when to fire. Android's alert is a private service that decides on its own, through an algorithm, within seconds. The IT-alert site, for that matter, warns that it is not enough on its own and urges people to learn about the risks in their area. A quake hitting a seismic zone in Italy can therefore make Android phones ring even when no official message has gone out.
 Emergency alerts attract scammers too. The Japanese disaster-alert service Arcadia was used to send 1.4 million phishing emails , and the false alarm about the worldwide blackout of November 17 started from a simple FEMA alert test . Android's alert needs no app and no link to be switched on, so anyone offering a "program to enable it" is selling something else.
 How to Check the Alert on Your Phone
 The check takes less than a minute, though menu labels can differ slightly from one manufacturer to another.
 Open Settings on your Android phone.
 Go to Safety & emergency (on some devices the entry sits under Location, then Advanced).
 Tap Earthquake alerts. If the "not supported in this region" badge is gone, the service is active.
 Use "See a demo" to view the three screens, including the full-screen one (to make sense of the other icons that show up at the top, there is the guide to the meaning of iPhone and Android icons ).
 Make sure location is on and that you have a Wi-Fi or mobile data connection.
 If the entry is not there yet, the rollout is still in progress. Updating Google Play Services from the Play Store can speed things up, even though the app does not turn up in search and normally updates itself. The most common reaction among people who got the strongest alert, Google reports, was Drop, Cover and Hold On, meaning get down, take cover and hold tight. The system is worth those few seconds, spent getting off a staircase or moving away from dangerous objects. Real time, brief as it is.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 1. Does it work on iPhones?
 No. The system is part of Android and Google Play Services, and Google's announcements mention only Android users. iPhones stay outside this service.
 2. Does Google know exactly where I am?
 No. According to Google Research the alerts rely on an approximate location, designed to protect privacy. Location is still required to receive the alert, and you stop contributing to detection by turning off Google Location Accuracy.
 3. What happens if Do Not Disturb is on?
 It depends on the level. The Take Action alert can override Do Not Disturb, wake the screen and ring loudly. Be Aware is a vibration-only notification and can go unnoticed.
 4. Does it work when I am abroad?
 It depends on the country. Since October 15 the covered regions number more than 200, but the up-to-date list is on Google's help page and is worth checking before a trip.
 5. Can I turn the alerts off?
 Yes. From the same Earthquake alerts page they can be switched on and off whenever you like. Google enables them by default.
